newsitem.title: USA: OMB's Minarik-FY97 revenue stream stronger than 96.
newsitem.headline: OMB's Minarik-FY97 revenue stream stronger than 96.

text.p: The government revenue stream coming in in fiscal year 1997 is stronger than was seen in fiscal '96, U.S. Office of Management and Budget Associate Director Joseph Minarik said Friday.

"... Revenues have been coming in stronger than we anticipated, and spending on Medicare and ... Medicaid have been lower. So, on balance, ... the deficit has been lower. If you take those trends and extrapolate them ... they would make for a lower budget deficit baseline," he told Reuters Financial Television.

"Relative to where we were at the end of fiscal '96, the revenue stream looks a little bit stronger. ... The stream is coming on the positive side from the individual and corporate income taxes. Some of the miscellaneous receipts have been coming in lower but those are things like the exact timing of payments for receipts from the government spectrum auctions and those of course are much more irregular and don't really reflect what's going on in the underlying economy," he added.
"There's not much of an opportunity to cut $150 billion in deficit in 2002 without touching pretty much some of everything," he said when asked about chances for cutting the budget deficit.

Asked if the White House would be more aggressive on entitlement spending and if there were room for significant new cuts in non-defense discretionary spending, Minarik said "I suspect the policies we'll be looking at will be pretty much like the ones we did last time because ... the economic forecasts do appear to be converging on where we were before.

"The tricky part of it is that we haven't gotten one year of head-start that we expected last year when we put together our budget plan. So, in one sense, the economy and the underlying numbers are getting better, but on the other hand we have a little bit less time to get there.

"So we're probably going to be about where we were last time. I don't anticipate any major changes in the character of the proposals we're putting forward but you'll have to do about as much lifting as you did last time ... probably to get a balanced budget in five years instead of six," he said.
